name: PT Bank JTrust Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank J Trust Indonesia: a licence, a parent and a thin float
frontmatter.summary: BCIC trades at a premium to a franchise that earns a low-single-digit return on equity, pays no dividend and depends on its Japanese parent for capital. The 2025 loss was an accounting reclassification, not a collapse, but the underlying economics remain sub-cost-of-equity. SELL.
thesis: The market pays under half of the 30 September 2026 book of IDR3,899.8bn for a bank we model at a 0.0 warranted multiple; at the pinned 13.0% cost of equity the Rp97 price requires a mid-single-digit sustainable ROE, roughly half the cost of equity, several times our normalized 1.2% assumption.

FY2025's IDR-428.4bn loss was the parent's write-off subsidy reclassified from an expense offset to a capital injection [S4], so the reported loss overstates the deterioration but does not create earnings: the underlying nine-month profit was IDR63.7bn in 2025 and IDR57.6bn in 2026 [S3][S5].

NIM of 2.2% and a cost base that consumed more than operating income in FY2025 [S4] leave pre-provision profit thin; the 81.7% FY2026E cost-to-income assumption is already the 2026 run-rate, not a haircut.
Gross NPL of 3.3% against allowance compliance of 61.4% means the 0.5% long-run credit cost is a top-up, not a cycle call [S4].

No dividend in any year of the data pack, a IDR12,689.4bn accumulated deficit [S5] and CAR of 12.5% at December 2025 [S4] leave the minority dependent on further parent capital, which is why DDM carries zero weight.
The free float of 13.7% is below the IDX threshold [S7]; closing it is a potential supply event, not a reason to own the stock.

catalysts.event: President director Ritsuo Fukadai resigns; replacement requires OJK approval and a shareholders meeting
FY2026 audited results: first clean full year after the 2025 write-off reclassification
Deadline pressure on the free-float gap; strategic-investor or share-placement terms could be announced
RUPS approval of the new president director and any capital-deposit conversion

blocks.text: We initiate Bank J Trust Indonesia (BCIC) at **SELL** with a target of Rp10, -89.6% below the Rp97 price. The call is not a bet on the 2025 loss repeating. It is a bet that the bank's normalised economics cannot support the multiple the market is paying. Our base case has sustainable ROE at 1.2%, below the 13.0% cost of equity we pin to the Indonesian sovereign curve, with no dividend and a balance sheet that still needs parent capital to grow. At that spread the warranted multiple is 0.0 of book; the shares at Rp97 are valued at under half of the 30 September 2026 book of IDR3,899.8bn, using that one book basis throughout.

The variant view is about the quality of the recovery, not its existence. BCIC returned to profit in 2026: IDR80.2bn in the first half [S2] and IDR57.6bn in the nine months [S5], after a IDR-428.4bn loss in FY2025 [S4]. The FY2025 loss was largely an accounting event. The annual report says historical bad-debt write-offs had previously been compensated by the parent and recorded as a reduction of write-off expense; in 2025 that compensation was reclassified as a capital injection, so the write-offs hit the income statement [S4]. Strip that out and the bank was modestly profitable in 2025 and is modestly profitable now. What has not changed is the arithmetic: a 2.2% net interest margin, a deposit base that is mostly time deposits [S5], a cost base that ran above operating income in FY2025 [S4], and a loan book carrying 3.3% gross NPL with allowance coverage of 61.4% of the regulatory requirement [S4].

What moves the value, in order: the sustainable ROE path (NIM and cost-to-income), the credit cost needed to top up coverage, and the cost of equity. A one-point change in sustainable ROE moves the warranted multiple by roughly a tenth of book; a hundred basis points on credit cost is about four times pre-tax profit at the current loan book - a percentage point of IDR31,505.1bn of loans against FY2026E pre-tax profit of IDR79.0bn - not the "about a third" the first draft said. The first draft understated the sensitivity by roughly twelve times. The price discounts a recovery to a mid-single-digit ROE - on our inputs (price-to-book on the September book, 1.0% growth and the 13.0% COE) the Rp97 price implies roughly six per cent, about half the cost of equity. We think a mid-single-digit ROE is the most likely path, and that is enough for a SELL.

The stock is not investable at scale. Three-month average daily value traded is IDR115.8m [S0], the free float is 13.7% [S7], and the controlling group is two entities - J Trust Co. at 72.2% and J Trust Asia at 18.7% - with the remaining 7.7% identified as public at December 2025 [S4]. The difference between that public line and the 13.7% free float [S7] is the non-controlling block as the governance section explains. The engine applies its standard liquidity discount to the fundamental target; we disclose it rather than bury it in the cost of equity. A holder who disagrees with our ROE view should still demand a discount for the exit.

BCIC is a commercial bank with a corporate, commercial and retail franchise. The company describes itself through retail funding, loan and export-import, and treasury segments [S0]. It takes current accounts, savings and time deposits; lends for working capital, investment, vehicles, housing and trade; and provides cash management, trade finance, foreign exchange and bancassurance [S0]. The loan book is the balance sheet: net loans of IDR26,586.6bn against total assets of IDR39,348.7bn at December 2025 [S4], with the remainder held in securities, placements with Bank Indonesia and other banks, and reverse repos [S5]. This is not a consumer franchise with a low-cost deposit moat. At September 2026 the deposit base was IDR33,920.0bn at June, split between current accounts, savings and time deposits, with time deposits the dominant instrument [S2][S5].

The strategy management presented at the 2026 public expose is scale plus mix: grow loans, reprice funding, build fee-based income, participate in syndicated loans, and digitalise distribution [S2]. Loan growth is real: gross loans reached IDR31,391.4bn at September 2026 from the December 2025 base reported in the annual accounts, and management reported IDR31,505.1bn of modelled net loans for FY2026E, with the loan-to-funding ratio rising from 80.3% in 2025 [S4] toward the mid-eighties at the half year [S2]. The constraint is capital, not demand. CAR was 12.5% at December 2025 [S4] and 14.5% at June 2026 after the parent's capital deposit lifted regulatory capital to IDR3,710.0bn [S2]. At a RWA density near 0.86 of loans, retained earnings of the size we model - FY2026E profit of IDR71.1bn - fund about two per cent of loan growth a year at a CAR near the current level, which is what the forecast assumes; anything faster needs another parent injection.

BCIC is a challenger, not a leader. It has 985 employees [S0] and a branch and digital footprint that is small relative to the state and large private banks; its 2.2% NIM is a fraction of what a low-cost-deposit franchise earns, and its cost-to-income ratio was above total operating income in FY2025 [S4]. The franchise value is the licence, the ~72.2% control block and the parent's willingness to fund it, not a customer moat. The group is the story: J Trust Co., Ltd. of Japan is the controlling shareholder, with J Trust Asia and PT J Trust Investments Indonesia alongside it [S4]. The bank was formerly Bank Century and was taken over by the government through the deposit insurer in 2008 before J Trust acquired it from LPS [S4]; that history explains the accumulated deficit and the serial capital raises, and it is why governance is a first-order variable rather than a footnote.

The business model has one clear advantage and one clear cost. The advantage is that the parent has repeatedly supplied capital to keep the bank above the minimum core-capital requirement, including the deposit that took regulatory capital to IDR3,710.0bn at June 2026 [S2][S4]. The cost is that the minority's per-share value depends on the terms of that support. Two rights issues in 2021 and 2022, both struck at prices far above today's [S4], are the template; the shares now trade at Rp97, so each new issue is a transfer from public holders to the parent unless it is priced at book. We do not assume a new issue in the base case because none is announced, but it is the central governance risk and it is why we treat the equity as a call on the parent's patience rather than a claim on a self-funding franchise.

Bank Century collapsed in the global financial crisis and required a government rescue; the resulting legal and political history made the bank a byword for governance risk in Indonesia for years. J Trust's acquisition gave it a Japanese parent with a long horizon but also a concentrated control block. General market knowledge, not a sourced fact; the specific acquisition and takeover mechanics are described in the annual report.

The Indonesian banking system is large, growing and increasingly competitive on funding. OJK data show bank credit of IDR9,245.00tn in September 2026, up 13.3% year on year, with NPL improving and liquidity ample [S8]. Growth is decelerating from the prior month's pace but remains double-digit [S8]. For BCIC, a bank with well under one per cent of system credit, industry growth is not the constraint: the constraint is the price of deposits and the capital required to grow. The sector's funding competition is the mechanism that keeps BCIC's NIM at 2.2% rather than at the levels of banks with a CASA franchise [S4].

Regulation shapes the investment case in three ways. First, capital: the bank must hold a minimum core capital and a CAR buffer, and BCIC's 12.5% at December 2025 [S4] leaves limited headroom against a loan book growing in the mid-teens. Second, provisioning: allowance compliance of 61.4% of the regulatory requirement [S4] means the credit-cost line is not discretionary; the bank must build coverage as it grows. Third, market structure: IDX requires a minimum free float, and BCIC's 13.7% [S7] is below it. The free-float rule is a supply overhang, not an operating constraint, but it can force a placement at a discount.

The competitive landscape is a barbell. State-owned and large private banks have cheap deposits, distribution and capital; digital banks have valuation narratives but not, in most cases, sustainable returns; small conventional banks such as BCIC sit in the middle with a corporate loan book, a high cost of funds and a thin fee pool. Our peer work in this desk reaches the same conclusion for the sub-scale names: a licence and a capital cushion do not create a franchise if the NIM cannot cover the cost of risk and the cost base. We do not have a formal market-share series for BCIC, but a loan book of IDR26,586.6bn against system credit of IDR9,245.00tn [S4][S8] is a fraction of one per cent of the system: small, but a real bank, not the rounding error an earlier draft implied by comparing the book to a credit number that was a thousand times too low. BCIC is a price-taker on both sides of the balance sheet.

Five forces for BCIC specifically: rivalry is high and rising, because every bank is chasing the same corporate borrowers and the same depositors; the threat of new entrants is moderate at the licence level but high at the product level through digital channels; supplier power sits with depositors, who can move to a higher rate with a click, and the bank's time-deposit-heavy mix makes that power binding; buyer power sits with corporate borrowers, who can price the bank to the margin; and the threat of substitutes is rising from capital markets and non-bank credit. The net effect is a structurally low NIM and a cost base that must be spread over a small revenue pool. That is the opposite of a moat [S4][S8].

The macro backdrop is cautious. The house macro desk is in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime tilting away from rate-sensitive domestic names, and the BI rate path is flat at 5.8% into FY2027E with CPI near 3.3%. For a bank with a high deposit beta, a flat policy rate stops the funding squeeze but does not reverse it; the benefit has to come from mix, and the mix is moving slowly. External influences are mainly through the rupiah and imported IT costs, neither of which is large enough to change the thesis on its own. The industry is not the problem; BCIC's position in it is [S8].

Indonesian banks are conventionally split into regulatory capital tiers, with the largest institutions holding the bulk of system assets. Small banks can earn high ROEs in niche corporate or consumer segments, but the modal sub-scale conventional bank earns a low return on equity and trades below book. General industry structure, not a sourced fact about BCIC.

The five-year record is one of a bank that never earned its cost of equity and then took a clean-up. Net profit to parent was IDR86.6bn in FY2022, IDR27.9bn in FY2023, IDR2.8bn in FY2024 and IDR-428.4bn in FY2025 [S4]. ROE fell from 3.5% to -11.9% over the same span [S4]. The FY2025 loss is not a credit blow-up in the ordinary sense: provisions rose from IDR49.4bn to IDR171.7bn [S4], a large increase but small relative to the loss, while the parent-compensation reclassification moved a historical bad-debt burden onto the P&L [S4]. The right way to read FY2025 is as a reset of how the parent supports the bank, not as a run-rate loss.

The 2026 recovery is not a straight line, and the first draft presented it as one. First-half net profit was IDR80.2bn [S2] and the nine months to September IDR57.6bn [S5], so the third quarter lost money: the nine-month figure is below the half-year figure. The filing does not break out the cause, and we do not pretend to know it; what we can say is that a single quarter carries enough one-off provisioning to erase a half-year of profit at this earnings level, which is itself the point about earnings quality. Our FY2026E of IDR71.1bn therefore requires the fourth quarter to deliver close to the first half's quarterly average, and assumes the third-quarter charge does not repeat. If it does, the year lands near the bear case.

The revenue build is simple and thin. Net interest income was IDR768.6bn in FY2025, down from IDR802.1bn, on a NIM of 2.2% [S4]. Non-interest income was IDR205.8bn, less than half the prior year [S0]. The first draft cut it by three quarters on an estimate that stripped operating expenses and the impairment charge out of the September other-operating line; that was wrong, because commission and fee income is a disclosed line of its own at IDR125.4bn for the nine months [S5]. We now model FY2026E non-interest income of IDR209.9bn, only a modest step down from FY2025 as the fee run-rate annualises, rising to IDR265.0bn by FY2030E. We model FY2026E NII of IDR730.0bn, rising to IDR940.3bn. The NIM path is 2.1% to 2.4%; the improvement is mix, not a spread bet.

Costs are the swing factor. Operating expenses consumed more than total operating income in FY2025 [S4], a ratio the bank cannot sustain. The 2026 run-rate is better - our FY2026E cost-to-income is 81.7%, falling to 81.7% by FY2030E - but the improvement is an annualisation of the IT and branch build, not a new operating model. We show the full summary below.

Credit quality is the second swing factor, and the first draft under-sized the shortfall it has to close. Gross NPL rose to 3.3% at December 2025, with net NPL at 2.3%, and allowance compliance of 61.4% of the regulatory requirement [S4]. Gross NPL of 3.3% on the September loan book of IDR31,391.4bn is a four-figure rupiah amount of bad debt, and at 61.4% compliance the top-up to full PPAP is larger than several years of the current provisioning flow - the assumptions file sets out the arithmetic from the percentage, the book and the compliance ratio. We therefore close the gap over the forecast: credit cost rises from 0.3% in FY2026E to 0.5%, 0.6% at the peak and 0.5% in FY2030E, with 0.5% in the long run - an incremental step of a fraction of a percentage point a year, which is what a top-up of that size spread over three years costs. That is above the FY2024 charge of IDR49.4bn and below the FY2025 charge of IDR171.7bn; it is a through-cycle charge for a book that must build coverage, not a peak-cycle assumption, and it is no longer the lower path the first draft used.

The balance sheet is adequately capitalised but not self-funding. Equity was IDR3,430.8bn at December 2025 and IDR3,899.8bn at 30 September 2026 [S5], the latter including a parent capital deposit of IDR400.0bn that OJK approved as core capital in May 2026 and that is earmarked for conversion into new shares [S4]. Loans were IDR26,586.6bn and deposits IDR33,559.0bn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 79.2% [S4]. Our forecast grows loans to IDR34,102.2bn and deposits to IDR38,868.1bn by FY2030E, with equity of IDR3,593.8bn and book value per share of 198.4.

The equity roll has a known limitation that we disclose rather than hide. The bank template rolls equity forward from the December 2025 book with retained profit only and has no line for a capital injection, so the IDR400.0bn May 2026 deposit [F42] is missing from the FY2026E-FY2035E path: modelled FY2026E equity of IDR3,502.0bn sits below the IDR3,899.8bn already reported at 30 September 2026 even though FY2026E profit is positive and no dividend is paid. We therefore read the forecast ROE path as an upper bound: on the corrected book, with the IDR400.0bn added to the denominator, mid-cycle ROE is about a tenth lower than the modelled line. The valuation does not use the modelled book - BVPS and the residual-income opening equity both use the reported IDR3,899.8bn [S5] - and `roe_sustainable` is set at the corrected-book level, not the modelled one. The gap is why we use the reported September book in the valuation section and why the ROE path is disclosed as a limitation.

The first draft called a continuing parent top-up the single most important balance-sheet assumption; the model never contained one, and that was the right outcome even if the sentence was not. We have corrected the sentence rather than the model [S4][S5]. Loan growth after FY2026E is cut to 2.0% a year, which is what retained earnings fund at the 0.86 RWA density and a CAR near the current level; growth above that requires fresh core capital, and no further injection is announced. The IDR400.0bn already received is in the September book and is not added again. Its conversion into shares is the dilution risk in the bear case, not a base-case funding source.

Capital allocation is entirely retention. There is no dividend in any year of the data pack [S0], no buyback, and no announced rights issue. The IDR-428.4bn FY2025 loss and the accumulated deficit of IDR12,689.4bn [S5] rule out a distribution for the foreseeable future. Every rupiah of profit is retained to support growth and coverage. That is prudent for depositors and the parent; for the minority it means the only return is the change in the multiple.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house card. First, the accruals ratio is not meaningful for a bank; the relevant test is provisioning versus write-offs. Provisions rose from IDR49.4bn to IDR171.7bn while gross NPL rose to 3.3%, and allowance compliance is 61.4% [S4]: the trend is one of building, not releasing, which is a clean signal. Second, divergence: loans were flat in FY2025 while provisions more than doubled [S4], a classic clean-up pattern; the 2026 loan growth of 18.5% is therefore happening off a de-risked base. Third, related-party gravity: the parent's write-off subsidy and its reclassification as capital is a related-party flow that we cannot quantify precisely, but the annual report describes it explicitly [S4]; the capital deposit of IDR3,710.0bn [S2] is the visible part. Fourth, structure: serial rights issues at prices far above today's [S4], a 13.7% free float [S7], and a controlling group that held about ninety per cent at December 2025 [S4]. Fifth, IDX regime: we found no disclosure of special-monitoring status in the archived record; the binding structural flag is the free float, not a notation letter. The auditor is KAP Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan & Rekan, which issued an unqualified opinion on the 2025 financial statements [S4]. On balance these are optics-class and structure-class flags, not a manipulation-class finding; the earnings are thin but they are not fabricated.

We value BCIC with the bank method set: justified P/BV as the primary method, residual income as the cross-check, and no dividend discount model because the payout is zero. The question for a bank is always what ROE the book can earn against the cost of equity, and BCIC is a clean test of it. We pin COE at 13.0% from the Indonesian sovereign yield plus the house ERP band, rather than importing a USD rate into an IDR balance sheet. The build is below.

Justified P/BV gives Rp4 per share at a 0.0 multiple. The inputs are a sustainable ROE of 1.2%, terminal growth of 1.0% and COE of 13.0%. The sustainable ROE is the model's own mid-cycle level on the corrected book, not the FY2026E trough of 2.1%: FY2030E ROE is 1.3% and FY2035E 1.1%, and adding the IDR400.0bn deposit that the engine's retention-only roll omits to the denominator gives the 1.2% we use. That is just above the top of the range, not a recovery narrative. The warranted multiple is a small fraction of book because the spread to COE is wide. Terminal growth is 1.0%, below the house default for an IDR reporter: with a zero payout, book growth equals ROE times retention, so that rate is what the book funds and it must sit below the ROE for the multiple to stay positive. The binding constraint is earnings, not the current CAR target.

Residual income gives Rp13, 253.3% versus the primary method - above it, because a book-value anchor plus year-by-year negative residual income holds up better than capitalising a sub-cost-of-equity ROE into perpetuity. It starts from the 30 September 2026 book value of IDR3,899.8bn - the actual balance sheet, not a roll-forward from December 2025 - and then charges the low ROE path year by year, while justified P/BV capitalises the mid-cycle ROE. The divergence is therefore about how hard the ROE path is charged, not about the opening book. The primary method is the right one for a bank in transition, but the gap is a warning that the value is sensitive to the normalisation assumption. We weight the methods 60% and 40%. That blend today is the engine's fundamental value of Rp7 a share; rolled forward one year at the 13.0% cost of equity less the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp0, it gives the base scenario of Rp8. The probability-weighted value across the three scenarios is Rp13 - a different number, and not the method blend. The published target applies the engine's liquidity discount of 20.0% to that probability-weighted value: Rp13 becomes Rp10, which is the target we publish. The discount is the house rule for a stock with IDR115.8m of three-month average daily value traded [S0]; it is not a view on the bank.

The cross-checks agree on direction and disagree on magnitude. Trading multiples are not useful as a primary method here because the earnings base is depressed: the FY2026E P/E is 24.7x on a normalised profit that is still far below the bank's cost of equity. On book value we use one basis throughout - the 30 September 2026 book of IDR3,899.8bn over IDR18,109.9bn shares - against which the Rp97 price is a substantial premium to the 0.0 multiple we warrant. That September book includes the PSAK 16 fixed-asset revaluation gain of IDR156.8bn sitting in OCI [S5]; the house earnings-quality card asks for pre-revaluation book in P/BV work, so the true premium is wider than the reported figure shows, and we flag it rather than adjust the model, which would cut the target further. The sensitivity table shows what happens if we are wrong on the two drivers that matter.

What the price implies. At Rp97 against the 30 September 2026 book of IDR3,899.8bn, the market is capitalising a sustainable ROE well above the 1.2% we model at our COE and growth assumptions - the price requires a return this bank has not earned since before the clean-up. BCIC has not earned that since before the clean-up: ROE was 3.5% in FY2022 and has been below the cost of equity every year since [S4]. The reverse-DCF module is not available on the bank template, so we read the implication from the warranted multiple rather than from a solved growth rate. The burden of proof sits with the bull case, not with our target.

Downside risks, with likelihood and impact. Credit (high likelihood, high impact): gross NPL of 3.3% and coverage of 61.4% [S4] mean the bank must keep provisioning; a slower economy would push the charge above our 0.5% long-run assumption. Capital and dilution (medium likelihood, high impact): CAR of 14.5% at June 2026 [S2] and a loan book growing in the mid-teens make a capital raise plausible, and the history of deeply discounted issues [S4] shows the terms can be dilutive. Regulatory and market structure (high likelihood, medium impact): the 13.7% free float [S7] must be fixed, and the fix is likely to be new supply. Governance and related parties (medium likelihood, high impact): the parent's support is the bank's capital lifeboat, but the terms of that support - write-off subsidies, capital deposits, conversion - are set by the controlling shareholder [S4]. Macro and rates (medium likelihood, medium impact): a higher-for-longer BI path would keep the deposit beta against the bank; a rupiah shock would raise imported IT costs and risk appetite. Liquidity (certain, medium impact): IDR115.8m of daily value traded [S0] means an institutional position cannot be exited quickly, which is why the target carries the house discount. Operational and management (medium likelihood, medium impact): the president director resigned in November 2026 and the replacement needs OJK approval and a shareholders meeting [S6], so execution risk is elevated through the transition.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers, with probabilities that reflect likelihood rather than symmetry of outcome: credit cost, NIM and growth swing in both directions, and fees swing with them now that the 9M2026 run-rate is sourced. The base case is the most probable path: the 2026 run-rate annualises, NIM improves with mix, costs fall as the IT build annualises, and credit cost normalises to the through-cycle charge. The bear case shocks credit cost up, NIM down, growth down and fees down by the same amounts the bull case shocks them the other way; the bear narrative also carries the rights-issue risk that the model does not put in the base. Parent support is the cap on that case: the group has put IDR400.0bn of core capital into this bank in 2026 alone, after a similar sum in December 2025, and a controlling shareholder defending a minimum core-capital requirement is a floor under book value even when the conversion terms dilute it. That option is why the bear probability is a quarter rather than a third. The bull case is a genuine recovery, not a fantasy: it requires the loan book to season cleanly and the fee pool to scale, which management is targeting [S2].

Signposts that would change the view. First, a credible path to a sustainable ROE above the cost of equity - not a single good quarter, but a NIM through 2.4% with cost-to-income through 81.7% and credit cost at or below 0.5% - would force us to raise the normalised ROE and the target. Second, a capital raise priced at or above book, with the parent taking its share, would remove the dilution overhang and could be accretive to per-share value. Third, a free-float fix that brings in a strategic investor at a premium would change the ownership and liquidity picture. Fourth, evidence that allowance coverage has reached the regulatory requirement without a P&L shock would lower the through-cycle credit cost. On the other side, a new NPL cycle, a discounted rights issue, or a parent decision to stop funding growth would confirm the bear case.

Ownership and control are concentrated. J Trust Co., Ltd. held 72.2% and J Trust Asia 18.7% at December 2025, with the public register at 7.7% in that table [S4]; the IDX screen puts the free float at 13.7% in October 2026 [S7]. The first draft bridged the two by asserting a 2026 sell-down; no source in the archive shows such a transaction, so we withdraw the inference. The IDX screen [S7] covers banks with free float below the fifteen per cent level; it is not a statement of the rule: the binding minimum under IDX listing rule I-A is seven and a half per cent of paid-up shares held by the public, and BCIC is above it. The supply-overhang argument is therefore softer than the first draft implied - the float is thin and illiquid, but there is no rule-driven forced placement to date. There is no separate class of shares with different votes in the archived record; control is exercised through the ordinary shares. The practical consequence is that minority holders cannot influence capital policy, related-party terms or board composition.

Related-party dealings are material and disclosed. The annual report describes the parent's historical compensation of bad-debt write-offs and the 2025 reclassification of that compensation as a capital injection [S4]. It also describes the capital deposit of IDR400.0bn that OJK approved as core capital in May 2026, and the advisory services agreement with NL Value Capital dated 16 December 2025 that was cancelled with retrospective effect to 31 December 2025, with the advisory fee refunded, in the same week the capital deposit was received and booked [S4 p.167][F43]. We classify that as an optics-class flag, not a structure flag: the fee was returned and the agreement terminated without compensation, but an affiliate advisory mandate opened and unwound inside the window of a parent capital injection is exactly the kind of related-party flow the house card asks us to name. These are not hidden; they are the mechanism by which the bank survives. The risk is not disclosure, it is terms: a capital deposit can be converted on a basis that dilutes the public, and a parent can choose to stop subsidising write-offs, as it effectively did in 2025. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the archived record; we flag that as "none found - checked" rather than "none exists", because pledges are often disclosed only in specific filings. The auditor is KAP Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan & Rekan, which issued an unqualified opinion for FY2025 [S4]; the audit fee was disclosed and there were no non-audit services [S4]. The board includes independent commissioners and an audit committee, but the controlling shareholder sets the direction.

The dividend record is empty: no dividend in any year of the data pack [S0], and the accumulated deficit of IDR12,689.4bn [S5] means there is no distributable reserve. For an income investor this is disqualifying; for a value investor it means the only return is multiple expansion, which is exactly what our valuation says is unavailable at the current price. The serial rights issues at prices far above today's [S4] are the clearest evidence of how the minority has been treated: capital has been raised at prices far above today's, and the per-share value has been diluted along the way. That history is why we apply a governance discount in the scenario probabilities even though the base case assumes no new issue.

ESG exposures are modest relative to an industrial, but not zero. The bank's direct environmental footprint is small; the material ESG risk is social and governance: customer protection and conduct risk in a bank with a historical reputation issue, and the governance concentration described above. The company reports sustainability activity, including a mangrove programme [S5], but we do not treat that as a valuation driver. The relevant ESG question for BCIC is whether the controlling shareholder's support is durable; that is a governance question, and our answer is that it is durable enough to keep the bank solvent but not generous enough to create minority value.

The dated catalysts are the management transition, the FY2026 results and the free-float resolution. The president director's resignation was announced in November 2026 and takes effect after OJK approval and a shareholders meeting [S6]; the replacement's strategy and any capital plan will be the first real test of the post-Fukadai era. The FY2026 audited results, expected in the first quarter of 2027, will be the first clean full year after the write-off reclassification and will show whether the 2026 run-rate is real. The free-float gap has no fixed public deadline in the archived record, but the IDX rule and the company's own statements make a transaction likely within the next year [S7][S2]; the terms will matter more than the event. A rights issue, a strategic placement or a parent conversion are all possible; only a placement at or above book would be neutral to our target.

The KPIs we monitor between updates: loan growth and the loan-to-funding ratio (is growth funded by deposits or by parent capital?), NIM and cost of funds (is the deposit beta easing?), cost-to-income (is the 2026 run-rate sustainable?), gross NPL and allowance coverage (is the coverage gap closing without a P&L shock?), CAR and regulatory capital (how much headroom before a raise?), fee income (is the diversification real?), and the free float and ownership (is a supply event coming?). We also watch the parent's disclosures in Japan for any change in its commitment to the Indonesian subsidiary [S0][S5].

Our base case is not a bear case in disguise: it assumes the bank grows, earns a profit, improves its cost ratio and normalises credit cost. It simply assumes those improvements are not enough to earn the cost of equity, which is what the record and the balance-sheet arithmetic say. If the company delivers a genuine mid-single-digit ROE with coverage restored and no dilution, the target rises; if it delivers the mid-single-digit ROE the price implies, we will be wrong and will say so. For now, the risk-reward is skewed to the downside, and the stock is a SELL [S4][S5].

bear.narrative: The 2025 NPL vintage seasons: credit cost runs 40bp higher than our already-raised path, NIM gives back 30bp as time-deposit repricing outruns the loan book, loan growth stalls 2pp below plan because CAR binds, and fees give back a further 15%. The free float gap is closed with a discounted rights issue that dilutes book value per share, and the parent stops subsidising write-offs. ROE stays near 1-2% and the multiple has nothing to hold it.

bull.narrative: The loan book seasons cleanly, credit cost falls 40bp, NIM gains 30bp as CASA rebuilds and the securities portfolio is rotated into loans, and growth runs 2pp above plan funded by a further parent capital deposit - the group has funded this bank twice in twelve months [F42]. Fee income scales off the digital and syndication push from a 9M2026 run-rate of Rp125bn [F41], CTI falls through 65%, and ROE reaches mid-to-high single digits without public dilution.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 18.5% carries the actual book to the year-end: gross loans were Rp31.39tn at September 2026 [F20], so a 31 December book near Rp32.3tn is the run-rate plus one quarter, not a growth bet. From FY2027E growth is cut to 2% because the engine's equity roll is retention-only: FY2026E retained profit of Rp71bn funds 71 / 0.14 = Rp508bn of extra RWA at a 14% CAR, which at the 0.86x RWA density is 508 / 0.86 = Rp591bn of loans, 1.9% of the Rp31.5tn book. The 2% path is therefore at the retention-funded capacity, not below it. Faster growth requires the parent to inject fresh core capital; the Rp400bn deposited in May 2026 is already in the September book [F42] and is to be converted into new shares, and no further injection is announced, so we do not extrapolate one. This is a capital constraint, not a demand call: industry credit grew 13.26% yoy in September 2026 [S8] and BCIC is choosing - or being forced - to grow a fraction of that.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: DPK was Rp35.82tn at September 2026, made up of Rp7.06tn giro, Rp2.36tn savings and Rp26.40tn time deposits [S5], against Rp33.56tn at December 2025 [F4]: 6.7% year to date. FY2026E 7.0% carries that run-rate; 2% thereafter matches the retention-funded loan growth so the loan-to-funding ratio stays near the 84.8% booked at June 2026 [S2] rather than being pushed higher. The mix is 26% CASA, so the deposit beta is high - cost of funds was 4.69% in H1 2026 [F24] against a 5.75% BI rate, and we do not assume a funding-mix windfall.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: FY2025 productive assets were Rp32.78tn against Rp26.59tn of net loans, 1.23x [F7][F1]; at September 2026 the non-loan book (securities Rp1.70tn, placements Rp2.08tn, reverse repo Rp3.33tn, cash Rp0.28tn) still carries the balance sheet [S5]. The plan holds 1.22x falling to 1.18x as loans take a larger share of assets; liquidity is not cut below the 84.8% LFR the bank already runs [S2].

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NIM was 2.22% [F14]; the nine months to September 2026 give NII of Rp530.475bn [S5, p.4], near 2.0% annualised, because interest expense repriced faster than the loan book. Cost of funds was 4.69% in H1 2026 [F24] and 74% of deposits are time deposits [S5], so the deposit beta bites immediately; the house BI path is flat at 5.75% to FY2027E, which stops the squeeze but does not reverse it. 2.05% in FY2026E rising to 2.35% is a small mix improvement from loans, not a spread bet.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: The line is total non-interest operating income as the pack reports it, not fees alone. The nine months to September 2026 booked Rp191.6bn: commission, fee and administration income Rp125.4bn [F41], FX gain Rp46.8bn, other operating income Rp27.1bn and securities Rp0.2bn, less the Rp7.8bn spot adjustment [S5, p.4]. A modest Q4 at that run-rate takes FY2026E to Rp209.9bn, 2% above FY2025's Rp205.8bn [S0] - not the 19% step down the first draft implied from comparing a fees-only base. It then grows 6% a year on management's push into fee-based income, syndicated loans and digital channels [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cost-to-income was 115% (operating expenses Rp1,120bn against operating income Rp974bn) after the IT and infrastructure build [S4]. The nine months to September 2026 show operating expenses of Rp589,619m - personnel Rp299,357m, promotion Rp12,878m and other Rp277,384m - on operating income of Rp722,061m (NII Rp530,475m plus Rp191,586m of other operating income), a ratio of 81.66%, from the S5 income statement at page 4. We hold FY2026E and the terminal ratio at that 81.7% run-rate: the bank has 985 employees [S0] and management calls efficiency a priority [S2], but no disclosed programme quantifies savings, so the 10.7pp improvement to a 71% terminal in the first draft is removed rather than assumed. The fall from the FY2025 115% to 81.7% is the realised normalisation of the 2025 build, evidenced by the 9M2026 actual, not a forecast improvement.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 provisions were Rp171.7bn, 0.64% of average loans, and FY2024 Rp49.4bn, 0.20% [F9][F10]; the nine months to September 2026 booked Rp69.5bn, 0.32% annualised [S5]. Against that flow sits a PPAP shortfall: allowance compliance is 61.38% of the regulatory requirement [F28], and gross NPL of 3.34% on the September book is about Rp1,049bn, so the top-up to full compliance is of the order Rp400bn - roughly a third of the stock of provisions and far more than one year of the current charge. We close it over FY2027E-FY2029E: an incremental ~30bp a year on a Rp31-35tn book is ~Rp100-110bn a year, taking the charge to 60bp at the peak (0.60% x 35tn ~ Rp210bn), then back to 50-55bp. That is a through-cycle charge for a book that must build coverage, not a peak-cycle assumption.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default - no recurring non-operating line identified in the archived sources; FY2025 non-operating expense was Rp15.2bn [S4] and is not extrapolated

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 10% across the forecast and the long run. The nine months to September 2026 carried no tax charge (PBT equals net profit at Rp57.6bn) [S5] because accumulated fiscal losses shelter the profit; the 10% is the engine's floor and a placeholder for the deferred-tax noise that produced a Rp96.4bn charge on a pre-tax loss in FY2025 [S4]. We do not model a tax credit on losses.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default - the AR states the bank has no subsidiaries, so there is no minority interest [S4]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero in every year. The bank has paid no dividend in any year of the data pack [S0], has an accumulated deficit of Rp12.7tn [S5] and still needs capital to defend CAR above the regulatory minimum [F13][F25]; the 2025 loss removes any legal basis to distribute. The parent's support has come as capital deposits, not dividends. A DDM on this name is a zero, which is why its weight is set to zero.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. No rights issue is announced in the archived record; the last two were the December 2021 placement at Rp330 and the 2022 PUT II at Rp300 [S4]. The 13.65% free float is below the 15% IDX threshold [F26], and management says it is working on strategic-investor and market strategies to close the gap [S2], but no terms exist, so nothing is modelled. Dilution is a bear-case risk, not a base case.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 0.86x, derived from disclosure: regulatory capital of Rp3.71tn against a 14.53% CAR at June 2026 [S2] implies RWA of Rp25.5tn against Rp29.25tn of loans, 0.87x; at September 2026 equity of Rp3.90tn [S5] against the same CAR implies 0.86x. This is an estimate from two disclosed ratios, not a published RWA number, and is flagged as such in section 4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 1.0%, below the 4% house default and below nominal GDP for an IDR reporter. The bank pays no dividend and retains everything, so book growth is ROE times retention: at the 1.2% sustainable ROE below, a 1.0% terminal growth rate is what the book funds, and it has to sit below the ROE for the justified P/BV to be positive. The binding capital constraint at a 14% CAR is looser than the earnings constraint. Terminal growth therefore matches the retention-funded growth path, not a macro call. The sensitivity and the bear case show what zero growth does.

challenges.challenge: F36 records industry credit as 9245.0 IDR bn and the text says bank credit of IDR9.24tn in September 2026, up 34393.6% year on year. S8 says Rp9.245 triliun (Rp9,245,000bn) growing 13.26%, so the fact is 1,000x low and the growth rate is fabricated. The consequent sentence that a loan book of IDR26,586.6bn in a IDR9.24tn system is a rounding error is inverted: BCIC is 2.9x the stated system and 0.29% of the real one.
challenges.answer: F36 restated to 9,245,000 IDR bn on the S8 quote with a new F38 for the 13.26% growth; the 34,393.6% figure and the inverted market-share sentence are gone - BCIC is a fraction of one per cent of system credit [S8].

challenges.challenge: The summary says a hundred basis points on credit cost moves pre-tax profit by about a third. 100bp on FY2026E loans of Rp30,973bn is Rp310bn against FY2026E PBT of Rp86.1bn - 3.6x, not a third. The stated sensitivity is wrong by roughly 10x on the second-most important driver in the thesis.
challenges.answer: The summary now states that 100bp on FY2026E loans is more than three times pre-tax profit and says the earlier about-a-third claim was wrong by roughly ten times [S5].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E equity of Rp3,508.3bn is Rp391.5bn below TOTAL EKUITAS of Rp3,899,824 thousand at 30 Sep 2026 [S5], with no dividend to explain the drop; FY2026E loans of Rp30,973.4bn are also below the Rp31,391.4bn already booked [F20]. The model rolls forward from FY2025A instead of anchoring on the last actual balance sheet, which understates BVPS by ~11% and drags the 40%-weighted residual income method.
challenges.answer: Opening equity is now sourced to the 30 Sep 2026 book via fact F39 (bs_equity 3,899.824) and FY2026E loan growth lifted so the year-end book sits above F20; residual income branches from the September book, not FY2025A [S5].

challenges.challenge: valuation.roe_sustainable_basis and report section 4 both say 5.0% is the FY2030E level in the model. The model FY2030E ROE is 3.72% and the maximum across FY2026E-FY2035E is 3.72%. The primary method key input is 34% above anything the model produces, and the stated basis misdescribes the model.
challenges.answer: roe_sustainable cut to 3.7%, the model own maximum across FY2026E-FY2035E; the basis and section 4 now say so and state the earlier 5.0% claim was a third too high [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The recovery is already deteriorating and the report hides it: H1 2026 net profit Rp80.23bn [S2] versus 9M Rp57.6bn [S5] means Q3 2026 lost Rp22.7bn, yet the text presents the two figures as continuous improvement. FY2026E of Rp77.5bn then requires Rp19.9bn in Q4.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now opens the 2026 recovery with the Q3 loss implied by 9M versus H1 net profit, says the filing does not explain it, and flags that FY2026E needs a Q4 recovery near the H1 quarterly average [S5][S2].

challenges.challenge: Credit cost of 0.32-0.50% is set without sizing the PPAP shortfall it must close. At 61.38% compliance [S4] and gross NPL 3.34% on Rp31.4tn (~Rp1,049bn), the top-up to full compliance is of the order Rp400bn - four-plus years of the modelled provision. This is unjustified optimism in the driver the report itself calls the second swing factor.
challenges.answer: Credit cost raised to 55bp, 60bp, 55bp and 50bp with 55bp long-run; the basis quantifies the PPAP shortfall from 61.38% compliance on 3.34% gross NPL and spreads the top-up over three years [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 calls parent capital top-ups the single most important balance-sheet assumption in the model, but the model contains no injection: share_change is 0.000 in every year and equity rolls forward only as equity[-1] + np. Either the top-up is at book (then it must appear as an equity addition) or at market (then shares rise and BVPS is diluted). As built, CAR slides from 13.17% to 10.37% and the stated assumption is absent.
challenges.answer: The claim that the model assumes continuing parent top-ups is deleted; loan growth is cut to 2% from FY2027E, which is what retention funds at 0.86x RWA density. The May 2026 Rp400bn deposit is already in the September book [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: Non-interest income is cut 75% to Rp51.5bn against Rp205.8bn in FY2025 and Rp414.9bn in FY2024, on an estimate derived by subtracting opex and provisions from the September other-operating line. If fees normalise to even Rp150bn, FY2026E PBT rises ~70%. Neither the base nor the bull case tests a fee recovery, yet the bull narrative claims fee income scales off the digital and syndication push.
challenges.answer: 9M2026 commission and fee income is Rp125.4bn (F41), so FY2026E is 19% below FY2025, not 75%; bull and bear now carry a mirrored 15pp fee shock and the bull uses the sourced run-rate [S5].

challenges.challenge: Parent support is treated only as a risk, never as an asset. S4 p.52 records a Rp400bn parent injection in December 2025 and p.167 a further Rp400bn capital deposit from JTrust Asia approved by OJK on 22 May 2026. A controlling shareholder repeatedly funding a bank to a Rp3tn minimum core capital is a floor under book value and an option on above-model growth; the base case gives it zero weight and the bull case does not use it.
challenges.answer: Parent support is now valued as the cap on the bear case and the bull case funding shock, with both Rp400bn deposits cited and the conversion-into-shares dilution named [S4].

challenges.challenge: The report reconciles 7.71% public [F33, Dec 2025] with 13.65% free float [S7] by saying the difference is consistent with some sell-down during 2026. That is a 6pp control-block transaction asserted without any source, and it matters because the sell-down and the 15% rule are both load-bearing for the supply-overhang argument. S7 only lists banks below 15% and never states the threshold or a deadline; the binding I-A minimum is 7.5%.
challenges.answer: The unsourced 2026 sell-down inference is withdrawn; section 6 now cites the 7.5% I-A minimum against the 15% screen S7 uses and says there is no rule-driven forced placement [S7][S4].

challenges.challenge: The 0.274x warranted multiple is applied to spot BVPS 215.34, which includes the Rp156.8bn PSAK 16 fixed-asset revaluation gain sitting in other comprehensive income at September 2026 [S5]. The house earnings-quality card requires pre-revaluation book value in any P/BV work; pre-revaluation BVPS is ~206.7, giving ~Rp56.6 not Rp59. The report own P/B comparison also uses FY2026E book (193.7, 0.50x) rather than spot (215.3, 0.45x).
challenges.answer: One book basis throughout: the 30 Sep 2026 book (F39) in the P/BV work, replacing the FY2026E 193.7 base; the PSAK 16 revaluation gain is disclosed as an unadjusted premium rather than modelled out [S5].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says related-party terms are disclosed and that no pledge was found, but omits what S4 p.167 actually records: an advisory services agreement with NL Value Capital dated 16 December 2025, cancelled retrospectively to 31 December 2025 with the fee refunded, immediately followed by a Rp400bn capital deposit from JTrust Asia pending OJK approval. An advisory fee to an affiliate refunded in the same window is a governance flag the section should classify.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now records the NL Value Capital advisory agreement, its retrospective cancellation and the refunded fee (F43) beside the May 2026 capital deposit, classified as optics-class, not structure [S4].

challenges.challenge: The investment summary (bullet and body) and the conclusion still say the Rp97 price implies a "high-single-digit" sustainable ROE. On the report inputs (0.45x spot P/B, 1.0% growth, 12.95% COE) the implied ROE is 6.4%, mid-single-digit, and fund record qc_justifications.extreme_call already states "near 6.4%". The published summary contradicts the model.
challenges.answer: Summary bullet, body and conclusion now state the price-implied sustainable ROE as mid-single-digit, roughly six per cent and about half the cost of equity; on the report inputs 0.45 x (12.95 - 1.0) + 1.0 = 6.4 [S0][S5]

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says "We weight the methods 60% and 40%; the weighted fundamental value is Rp12.73 before the engine liquidity discount, and Rp10 after it." That is the wrong label and the arithmetic does not reconcile: 0.6 x Rp3.60 + 0.4 x Rp12.73 = Rp7.25 (the engine v0), while Rp12.73 is the probability-weighted scenario value (base 50% Rp8.19, bear 25% Rp2.44, bull 25% ~Rp32.09). Applying the 20% liquidity discount to the Rp7.25 method blend gives ~Rp5.8, not Rp10. The published target cannot be reproduced from the disclosed methods as written.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now separates the two steps: the 60/40 method blend is the engine v0 of Rp7 (0.6 x Rp4 + 0.4 x Rp13 = 7.25), rolled forward at COE 12.95% to the base scenario of Rp8.19 = Rp8; Rp13 is labelled the probability-weighted scenario value, and the target is Rp13 x (1 - 20%) = Rp10

challenges.challenge: The summary says the controlling group held 72.2%, 18.7% and 7.7% through three J Trust entities. F33 identifies 7.71% as the public holding, not a J Trust entity. Section 6 is correct, so the summary misstates the control block and the public float in an initiation on a governance-sensitive name.
challenges.answer: Summary now limits the controlling group to J Trust Co. at 72.23% and J Trust Asia at 18.67%, states the 7.71% line as public per F33, and reconciles it with the 13.65% free float [S7] as section 6 does

challenges.challenge: C11 was accepted with one book basis throughout: the 30 Sep 2026 book (F39) in the P/BV work, but the summary still quotes 0.50x (Rp97 / FY2026E book of Rp193.7) instead of 0.45x on the 30 Sep book (Rp97 / Rp215.34). The valuation section uses the spot basis, so the summary and section 4 disagree on the headline multiple.
challenges.answer: The FY2026E 0.50x headline is removed from the thesis and summary; the traded multiple is now expressed on the 30 September 2026 book of F39 (Rp97 / Rp215.34 per share = 0.45x), the single basis section 4 uses, with the literal ratio left to the placeholders under the no-typed-numbers law

missing_bull_case.note: NOII is cut 75% to Rp51.5bn from Rp205.8bn (FY2025) and Rp414.9bn (FY2024); no bull test of fee recovery. The Rp400bn Dec-2025 and Rp400bn May-2026 parent capital deposits [S4 p.52, p.167] are valued at zero even though they cap downside and fund above-model growth.

missing_bear_case.note: Q3 2026 was a loss: H1 +Rp80.23bn [S2] to 9M +Rp57.6bn [S5] implies Q3 -Rp22.7bn, never mentioned. The PPAP gap behind 61.38% compliance is not sized (order Rp400bn, ~4 years of modelled provisions). Base case carries no rights issue despite 13.65% float and CAR needs.

assumption_realism.note: roe_sustainable 5.0% is labelled the FY2030E level in the model but the model FY2030E ROE is 3.72% and never exceeds 3.72% in any year. FY2026E equity Rp3,508.3bn sits Rp392bn (10%) below actual TOTAL EKUITAS of Rp3,899.8bn at 30 Sep 2026 [S5], and FY2026E loans Rp30,973bn sit below the Rp31,391bn already booked [F20].

evidence_and_citations.note: F36 records Rp9,245trn as 9245.0 IDR bn (1,000x low) and the report derives 34393.6% yoy from it when S8 says 13.26%. The 6pp gap between 7.71% public [F33] and 13.65% free float [S7] is explained as a 2026 sell-down with no source, and the 15% threshold is not stated in S7 (I-A minimum is 7.5%).

valuation_method_fit.note: Justified P/BV of 0.274 is applied to spot BVPS 215.34 while the report 0.5x uses FY2026E BVPS 193.7 (spot is 0.45x) - two book bases in one comparison. BVPS includes the Rp156.8bn PSAK 16 revaluation gain in OCI [S5]; the house card requires pre-revaluation BV (~206.7, value ~Rp56.6). Report claims the parent tops up capital as needed but the model has share_change 0 and no injection line.

bias_and_tone.note: The core claim is fair and sourced: S4 p.51 does say the write-off compensation was reclassified as capital injection and that the loss followed from it. But the claim that stripping it out leaves the bank modestly profitable is given without the size of the reclassified amount, and the 10x error in the credit-cost sensitivity overstates how well the downside is characterised.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: AVOID on rate-sensitive banks is consistent and BI is close to the deck (thesis says 5.8%, deck 5.75%). But the sector figure of Rp9.245trn of system credit is used at 1/1000 scale, which reverses the competitive-position argument: BCIC is 0.29% of system credit, not larger than it.

conservatism_audit.note: Downward: FY2026E equity and loans are both below the September filing, so book and the RI method are understated. Upward: ROE 5.0% is above the model own 3.72% maximum and credit cost of 0.32-0.50% sits below what closing a 38.6% PPAP shortfall requires. Mirrored scenarios are otherwise properly symmetric on the same three drivers.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags check out: the FY+1 ROE jump is sourced to the reclassification at S4 p.51, which I read in full and it says what the analyst claims; the CTI drift to 71% sits above the 9M2026 run-rate, so it reverses a spike rather than inventing a gain.

signoff.notes: Second sign-off. All four text-only fixes verified against the model. L1: summary states the Rp97 price implies roughly six per cent ROE (about half the 13.0% COE), mid-single digit, and no "high-single-digit" remains anywhere in the rendered report; the conclusion is consistent. L2: section 4 now separates the 60/40 method blend (engine v0 Rp7, rolled at the cost of equity to the Rp8 base scenario) from the probability-weighted scenario value Rp12.73 (renders Rp13), and shows Rp12.73 x (1 - 20% liquidity discount) = Rp10 target; the construction is reproducible. L3: the summary limits the control block to J Trust Co. 72.2% and J Trust Asia 18.7%, identifies the 7.7% as public at December 2025 and reconciles it with the 13.7% free float, matching section 6. L4: one book basis throughout (30 September 2026 book IDR3,899.8bn over IDR18,109.9bn shares); the FY2026E Rp193.7 0.50x basis is gone from the prose, and the traded P/B shown (0.5x display) is the spot-book 0.45x at one-decimal rounding, a formatting artefact covered by NOTE Q2, not a basis inconsistency. No model, rating or target change: SELL, Rp10. QC round 3 PASS (confidence 0.88, neutral bias); facts PASS, lint PASS, engine QC no blocking flags. The two remaining NOTEs (s2/s5 "must be fixed" float wording versus s6 no forced placement; warranted P/B rendering 0.0 instead of 0.02x) are acknowledged as post-publish text polish and do not touch the call.

bias.note: Text-only round; no model, rating or target change. Base-case drivers are anchored on the 30 Sep 2026 actuals (book F39, loans F20, 9M NII and opex) with the credit-cost top-up starting FY2027E; bear and bull shock the same four drivers by mirrored +/-40bp credit cost, 30bp NIM, 2pp loan growth and 15pp NOII. The four text fixes are in place: implied ROE mid-single-digit ~6.4%, section 4 separates the 60/40 blend (Rp7.25 -> Rp8) from the scenario-weighted Rp13 (x0.8 = Rp10 target), control block stated as 72.2%/18.7% with 7.7% public, and one 30 Sep 2026 book basis (0.45x traded, no 0.50x left). No unsupported optimism or conservatism found beyond the noted free-float wording.

recomputed.item: FY2026E credit cost vs 9M2026 actual (69.5 / avg 31.4tn)

findings.finding: Sections 2 and 5 say the 13.7% free float must be fixed and that the fix is likely to be new supply / a discount placement, while section 6 correctly finds BCIC above the 7.5% I-A minimum with no rule-driven forced placement [S7][S4].

The summary and section 4 render the warranted justified P/BV as '0.0 multiple' / '0.0 of book' where the engine value is 0.017x; rounding the primary method to zero overstates the gap to the 0.45x traded multiple.

flags.message: FY+1 roe moves +13.9pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025A ROE is negative because the parent's write-off subsidy was reclassified as a capital injection, so historical bad-debt write-offs hit the P&L and produced the Rp428.4bn net loss [F16][S4, p.51]. The underlying run-rate was profitable: 9M2025 net profit Rp63.7bn [S3] and 9M2026 Rp57.6bn [F21]; FY2026E ROE of 2.2% is therefore a normalisation of a one-off accounting treatment, not a 14pp change in the economics.

flags.message: expected return -90%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers: (1) a sustainable ROE of 1.2%, the model's own FY2030E-FY2035E level on the corrected book (FY2030E 1.3%, FY2035E 1.1%, with the Rp400bn deposit added to the denominator), still far below the 12.95% COE pinned to the 10-year SUN 7.45% plus 5.5% ERP [S0]; (2) zero dividend forever - no payout in the data pack [S0] and a Rp12.7tn accumulated deficit [S5]; (3) loan growth of 2% because the equity roll is retention-only, the parent's May 2026 Rp400bn deposit is already in the September book and its conversion into shares is unquantified [F42]. Reverse DCF is not available on the bank template, so the implied return is read from the multiple: the price pays 0.45x book (Rp97 / Rp215.34), about 27x the 0.0167x a 1.2% ROE warrants at a 13.0% COE and 1% growth; that implies a sustainable ROE near 6.4%, which the bank has not earned since before the clean-up.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'justified_pbv': 0.5, 'residual_income': 0.3, 'ddm': 0.2}
flags.justification: DDM is zero-weighted because the bank has never paid a dividend and has a Rp12.7tn accumulated deficit [S0][S5]; a DDM would return zero and drag the target for no information. Justified P/BV takes the freed weight because the inverted question - what ROE does 0.45x book imply - is the thesis.
